'''June Dalziel Almeida''' (5 October 1930 – 1 December 2007) was a [[Scottish people|Scottish]] [[virology|virologist]], a pioneer in virus imaging and identification. Her skills in electron microscopy earned her an international reputation.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/><ref name="NYT obit"/>

In 1964, Almeida was recruited by [[St Thomas's Hospital Medical School]] in London. By 1967, she had earned her [[Doctor of Science]] on the basis of her research and the resulting publications, while working in Canada, at Toronto's [[Ontario Cancer Institute]] and then in London at St Thomas's.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/> she then continued her research at the [[Royal Postgraduate Medical School]] (RPGMS),<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/> which later became part of the [[Imperial College School of Medicine]].

Almeida succeeded in identifying viruses that were previously unknown, including—in 1966—a group of viruses that was later named [[coronavirus]],<ref name="JGV_Almeida_1966" group="Publications"/><ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002"/>{{rp|96}} due to their [[crown]]-like appearance.<ref name=":0" /> Her [[immune electron microscopy]] (IEM) innovations and insights contributed to research related to the diagnosis of [[hepatitis B]], [[HIV]], and [[rubella]], among other viral diseases. Her electron micrographs continue to be included in virology review textbooks, decades after she produced them.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/>

==Early life==
Almeida was born on 5 October 1930 at 10 Duntroon Street, [[Glasgow]], to Jane Dalziel (née Steven) and Harry Leonard Hart, a bus driver.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418">{{Cite journal| volume = 336| issue = 7659| pages = 1511.1–1511| last = Almeida| first = Joyce| title = June Almeida (née Hart)| journal = [[The BMJ]]| publisher= [[BMJ Group]] | date = 28 June 2008| pmc = 2440895 | doi = 10.1136/bmj.a434 |bibcode = 1963Sci...142.1487A}}</ref>{{rp|1511.1–1511}}<ref name="Booss_August_2013"/><ref name="NYT obit">{{cite news |last1=Gellene |first1=Denise |title=Overlooked No More: June Almeida, Scientist Who Identified the First Coronavirus |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2020/05/08/obituaries/june-almeida-overlooked-coronavirus.html |newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=May 8, 2020 |quote=In 1966, she used a powerful electron microscope to capture an image of a mysterious pathogen — the first coronavirus known to cause human disease.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/|title=The Times & The Sunday Times|website=[[The Times]]}}</ref>{{Full citation needed|date=May 2020}} In 1940, her six-year-old brother died of [[diphtheria]], perhaps leading to her interest in diseases.<ref name=":0" />

In 1947, when she was 16, Almeida attended [[Whitehill Secondary School]] where she excelled academically winning the science prize.<ref name=":0" /> In 1947, when she was 16, she left school but was unable to attend university at that time due to financial constraints.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" /> She instead took up a position as a [[histopathology]] technician at  [[Glasgow Royal Infirmary]]. She was then recruited by a former colleague, Dr John W.S. Blacklock<ref name=":0" /> to do similar work at [[St Bartholomew's Hospital]]. She worked at St Bartholomew's until 1954.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" />

==Career==
===Ontario Cancer Institute===
In 1954, Almeida was hired for a newly opened position as [[Electron microscope|electron microscopy]] technician at the [[Ontario Cancer Institute]].<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/><ref name="Booss_August_2013"/>{{rp|209}}

While working as an electron microscopist, she and her Cancer Institute colleagues produced a series of studies applying negative staining to clinical problems.<ref name="Booss_August_2013"/>{{rp|209}}

In 1963, Almeida was the first of three authors of an article in the journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'', in which they identified virus-like particles in cancer patients' blood.<ref name="Science_Almeida_1963">{{Cite journal| access-date = 18 April 2020| url = https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.142.3598.1487 |title=Virus-Like Particles in Blood of Two Acute Leukemia Patients |first1=June D. |last1=Almeida |first2=Richard C. |last2=Hasselback |first3=Arthur W. |last3=Ham|journal=Science  |date=December 13, 1963 |volume=142 |number=3598 |pages= 1487–1489 |doi=10.1126/science.142.3598.1487 |pmid=14077540| bibcode = 1963Sci...142.1487A | s2cid = 21193415 |url-access=subscription }}</ref>  In the same year, she published her research in which she "negatively stained aggregates of antigen...and antibody" with the electron microscope.<ref name="JEM_Almeida_1963" group="Publications">{{Cite journal| pmc=2137656| doi = 10.1084/jem.118.3.327| issn = 0022-1007| volume = 118| issue = 3| pages = 327–340| last1 = Almeida| first1 = June| last2 = Cinader| first2 = Bernhard| last3 = Howatson| first3 = Allan| title = The Structure of Antigen-Antibody Complexes: A Study by Electron Microscopy| journal = Journal of Experimental Medicine | date = 1 September 1963| pmid = 14077994| doi-access = free}}</ref> Almeida's sense of humour arose in an ode to electron microscopy, and the symmetrical structure of [[Coronavirus disease|coronavirus]] (with an apology to poet, [[William Blake]]).<blockquote>“Virus, virus shining bright,

In the phosphotungstic night,

What immortal hand or eye,

Dare frame thy fivefold symmetry.”<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Scottish doctor found first human coronavirus case in 1960s|url=https://www.thenational.scot/news/18458272.scottish-doctor-found-first-human-coronavirus-case-1960s/|website=The National|date=19 May 2020 |language=en|access-date=2020-05-20}}</ref><ref name="NYT obit" /></blockquote>

===St Thomas's Hospital Medical School===
{{main|St Thomas's Hospital Medical School}}

In 1964, Tony Waterson, who had just been appointed as chair of microbiology at St Thomas's, met Almeida while visiting Toronto, and recruited her to join his research team<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002">{{cite book |date=2002 |title=Cold wars: the fight against the common cold |first1=David |last1=Tyrrell |first2=Michael |last2=Fielder |location=Oxford, England |publisher=Oxford University Press |pages=253}}</ref>{{rp|96}} at one of the oldest and most prestigious medical schools in the United Kingdom—[[London]]'s [[St Thomas's Hospital Medical School]], now part of [[King's College London]]. At St Thomas's, she worked on [[hepatitis B virus]] and the [[Common cold|cold viruses]].<ref name="ODNB_Banatvala_2011_01" />

In 1966, Waterson and Almeida collaborated with the physician and director of research on the common cold, David Tyrrell, who was working on a new organ culture system. Tyrrell's team had been attempting to detect the presence of [[rhinovirus]]es in tissue cultures of cells that they had produced in the lab. They wanted to detect a specific respiratory virus they called B814. The Swedish professor Bertil Hoorn could make all Tyrrell's respiratory viruses in organ cultures of cells from the human airway in the laboratory, except for virus B814. This organ culture system meant they did not have to depend on human volunteers to do research on these viruses. They wanted a reliable method to detect virus B814.<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002" />{{rp|94}}

By 1967, Almeida earned her [[Doctor of Science]] (DSc) based on her publications on electron micrographic research of antibodies conducted at the Ontario Cancer Institute and at St Thomas's.<ref name="Booss_August_2013" />{{rp|209}}

In the book ''Cold Wars'' (2002), which Tyrrell wrote with Michael Fielder, he described how when he first met Almeida she seemed to be extending the range of the electron microscope to new limits.<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002"/>{{rp|96}}

According to Tyrrell, prior to her innovative work, it was generally accepted that viruses had to be concentrated and purified to detect them with the electron microscope. When she told Tyrrell that she could "find virus particles" in the organ cultures that they had collected, with her "new, improved techniques", he was skeptical.<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002" />{{rp|96}}

Tyrrell's team sent samples to Almeida in London. These included a sample prepared with the B814 virus, along with samples infected with influenza and herpes, which were well known. When she examined the samples through her microscope grids, "she recognized all the known viruses, and her pictures revealed their structure beautifully. But more importantly, she also saw virus particles in the B814 sample."<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002" />{{rp|96}} she told Tyrrell that the B814 specimens had reminded her of particles she had previously studied in a "disease called infectious bronchitis of chickens" and in another disease—"mouse hepatitis liver inflammation." Almeida's papers on these had been rejected because the referees considered her [[electron micrograph]]s to be "bad pictures" of known influenza virus particles. Almeida told him she now knew that these "three viruses were something quite new."<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002" />{{rp|96}}

According to Tyrrell, once Almeida had identified the previously unrecognised group of viruses, they met in Waterson's office, to decide on its name. The viruses appeared to be surrounded by a "halo", which in Latin is "corona", and the name "coronavirus" was born.<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002"/>{{rp|96}}

In 1966, she and Tyrrell wrote that "The particles are pleomorphic, in the size range 800 to 1200 Å, and are surrounded by a distinct 200 Å long fringe. They are indistinguishable from the particles of avian infectious bronchitis, the only virus previously known to have this morphology."<ref name="JGV_Almeida_1966" group="Publications">{{Cite journal|last1=Almeida|first1=June D.|last2=Tyrrell|first2=D. A. J.|date=1967|title=The Morphology of Three Previously Uncharacterized Human Respiratory Viruses that Grow in Organ Culture|journal=Journal of General Virology|volume=1|issue=2|pages=175–178|doi=10.1099/0022-1317-1-2-175|pmid=4293939|issn=0022-1317|doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Royal Postgraduate Medical School of London (RPGMS)===
In 1968, Almeida published an article in ''[[Journal of General Virology]]'', on "avian infectious bronchitis virus".<ref name="JGV_Berry_Almeida_1968" group="Publications">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1099/0022-1317-3-1-97| issn = 0022-1317| volume = 3| issue = 1| pages = 97–102| last1 = Berry| first1 = D. M.| last2 = Almeida| first2 = June D.| title = The Morphological and Biological Effects of Various Antisera on Avian Infectious Bronchitis Virus| journal = Journal of General Virology| date = 1968| pmid = 5692879| doi-access = free}}</ref>

In 1971, using her immune electronmicroscopy technique, Almeida made the landmark discovery that the [[hepatitis B]] virus had "two immunologically distinct components"—an "outer coat and a small inner component".<ref name="Nahmias_2012">{{Cite book| publisher = Springer Science & Business Media| isbn = 978-1-4684-1012-9| last1 = Nahmias| first1 = André J.| last2 = O'Reilly| first2 = Richard J.| title = Immunology of Human Infection: Part II: Viruses and Parasites; Immunodiagnosis and Prevention of Infectious Diseases| date = 2012-12-06}}</ref>

===Wellcome Institute===
Almeida spent her final years of her professional career at the [[Wellcome Institute]] before she retired.<ref name="ODNB_Banatvala_2011_01">{{cite ODNB |first1=J. E. |last1=Banatvala |series=Almeida, June Dalziel (1930–2007) |title=Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |date= January 2011 |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/99332 |url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/99332 |access-date= 18 October 2012}}</ref> While working for the Institute she was named on several patents in the field of imaging viruses.<ref>{{Deprecated archive|url=https://archive.today/20130128013213/http://patent.ipexl.com/inventor/Almeida_June_Dalziel_1.html|title=Almeida, June Dalziel}}, patents, accessed October 2012</ref>

===Major contributions===
In their 2013 book entitled ''To Catch a Virus'', John Booss and Marilyn J. August describe how Almeida "played a crucial role in adapting the electron microscope to clinical diagnostic virology work."<ref name="Booss_August_2013">{{Cite book|last1=Booss|first1=John|chapter-url=https://archive.org/details/tocatchvirus0000boos/page/217|title=To Catch a Virus|last2=August|first2=Marilyn J.|publisher=ASM Press|year=2013|isbn=978-1-55581-507-3|location=Washington, DC|pages=197–249|chapter=Chapter 7: Imaging viruses and tagging their antigens|quote=ASM: "This chapter first examines the refinements in electron microscopy (EM) that greatly expanded the understanding of the structure and replication of viruses and facilitated the application of EM to viral diagnosis. The refinements included thin sectioning, negative staining, and immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) developed for clinical diagnostic work. The use of EM in discovering the viral causes of acute gastroenteritis and infectious hepatitis are then considered."|access-date=18 April 2020}}</ref>{{rp|209}}<ref group="Notes">In the chapter entitled "Imaging viruses and tagging their antigens" in John Booss and Marilyn J. August's 2013 ''To Catch a Virus'', they describe the how "refinements in electron microscopy (EM)...greatly expanded the understanding of the structure and replication of viruses and facilitated the application of EM to viral diagnosis. The refinements included thin sectioning, negative staining, and immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) developed for clinical diagnostic work. The use of EM in discovering the viral causes of acute gastroenteritis and infectious hepatitis are then considered." ASM: "This chapter first examines the refinements in electron microscopy (EM) that greatly expanded the understanding of the structure and replication of viruses and facilitated the application of EM to viral diagnosis. The refinements included thin sectioning, negative staining, and immunoelectron microscopy (IEM) developed for clinical diagnostic work. The use of EM in discovering the viral causes of acute gastroenteritis and infectious hepatitis are then considered."</ref>

Before Almeida's work with Anthony Peter Waterson in the 1960s,  few improvements had been made on the initial 1941 "proof of principle aggregation of virus by virus-specific antibody observable by [electron microscope (EI)]." In 1963, she pioneered a technique in [[immune electron microscopy]] (IEM), to better visualise viruses by using [[antibody|antibodies]] to aggregate them.<ref name="JEM_Almeida_1963" group="Publications"/> In the 1960s, she and Waterson were using [[negative staining]] for the EM of viruses—a technique that was both rapid and simple—and provided excellent detailed observations of viral morphology, which had revolutionized the electron microscopy of viruses overnight.<ref name="Booss_August_2013" />{{rp|208}}

In 1966, using her new techniques, Almeida was able to identify a group of "previously uncharacterised human respiratory viruses", while collaborating with [[David Tyrrell (physician)|David Tyrrell]],<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002"/>{{rp|96}}<ref name="Booss_August_2013"/>{{rp|209}} then director of the [[Common Cold Unit|Common Cold Research Centre]]<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/> in [[Salisbury]] in [[Wiltshire]].<ref name="BBC_Brocklehurst_20200415">{{Cite news|last=Brocklehurst|first=Steven|url=https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-scotland-52278716|title=The woman who discovered the first coronavirus|date=15 April 2020|work=BBC Scotland News|access-date=17 April 2020}}</ref> Tyrrell suggested calling the new group "coronaviruses". The coronavirus family of viruses now includes the [[SARS virus]]<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418"/> and the [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2|SARS-CoV2]] virus that causes [[Coronavirus disease 2019]].<ref name="Tyrrell_Fielder_2002"/>{{rp|96}}

In 1967, using the IEM aggregation method, Almeida produced the first visualisation of rubella virus.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" /><ref name="Lancet_Best_1967">{{Cite journal| doi = 10.1016/S0140-6736(67)92302-1| issn = 0140-6736| volume = 290| issue = 7509| pages = 237–239| last1 = Best| first1 = Jennifer M| last2 = Banatvala| first2 = J. E.| last3 = Almeida| first3 = June D| last4 = Waterson| first4 = A. P.| title = Morphological characteristics of rubella virus| journal = [[The Lancet]]| access-date =18 April 2020| date = 29 July 1967| url = https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(67)92302-1/abstract| url-access = subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Brilliant! Scottish inventors, innovators, scientists and engineers who changed the world|last=Paterson|first=Andrew|publisher=Austin Macauley|year=2017|isbn=9781786294357|location=London|pages=577}}</ref>

==In retirement==
After taking early retirement<ref name=":0" /> from Wellcome Institute, Almeida returned in an advisory role to St Thomas's. In the late 1980s she helped produce micrographs of the [[HIV virus]],<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" /> where [[University of Aberdeen]] professor of bacteriology [[Hugh Pennington]] was also then attached.<ref name=":0" />

Almeida's publications include the 1979 ''Manual for rapid laboratory viral diagnosis'' for the [[World Health Organization]].<ref name="WHO_Almeida_1979" group="Publications">{{Cite web|url=http://whqlibdoc.who.int/offset/WHO_OFFSET_47.pdf|title=Manual for rapid laboratory viral diagnosis|last=Almeida|first=June D.|date=1979|publisher=World Health Organization (WHO)}}</ref>

Almeida trained as a yoga teacher and became involved in her second husband Philip Gardner's antique business.<ref name="NYT obit" />

==Legacy==
In 1970, at the Royal Postgraduate Medical School (RPGMS) Almeida taught [[Albert Kapikian]] the technique of immune electron microscopy (IEM). Kapikian, who was visiting for six months from the United States [[National Institutes of Health]], used her techniques in the identification of a cause of non-bacterial gastroenteritis—the [[Norwalk virus]], now known as the Norovirus.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" /><ref name="ODNB_Banatvala_2011_01" />

Almeida's work received new attention during the early months of the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. Her little-known story was first published by the ''[[The Herald (Glasgow)|Herald]]'' in Scotland on 7 March 2020, the [[BBC]] on 15 April 2020<ref name="BBC_Brocklehurst_20200415" /> the ''[[National Geographic]]'' on April 17, 2020,<ref name="NatGeo">{{cite news|last1=Combs|first1=Sydney|url=https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/2020/04/june-almeida-discovered-coronaviruses-decades-ago-little-recognition/|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200418214024/https://www.nationalgeographic.com/history/2020/04/june-almeida-discovered-coronaviruses-decades-ago-little-recognition/|url-status=dead|archive-date=18 April 2020|title=She Discovered Coronaviruses Decades Ago—But Got Little Recognition|date=April 17, 2020|access-date=18 April 2020|publisher=[[National Geographic Society]]|agency=National Geographic}}</ref> and later her research noted in ''[[The National (Scotland)|The National]]''  on 19 May 2020.<ref name=":0" /> According to professor of bacteriology Hugh Pennington, Chinese scientists credited Almeida's work, including techniques she developed, with the early identification of [[coronavirus disease 2019]].<ref name="heraldscotland_20200307">{{Cite news|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/18289806.june-almeida-tribute-scotlands-forgotten-hero-coronavirus/|title=June Almeida, tribute to Scotland's forgotten hero of the coronavirus|date=7 March 2020|newspaper=Herald Scotland|access-date=18 April 2020}}</ref>

In 2025, an exhibition on the international endeavour to develop a [[COVID-19 vaccine]] opened at the [[National Museum of Scotland]], called ''Injecting Hope: The Race For A Covid-19 Vaccine'' showing the scientific principles and innovative research behind the urgent development of a vaccine and the global logistical challenges it faced. Almeida's original work underpinning the theory behind later research, is marked with her notebooks on exhibit.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2025-02-03 |title=Scottish museum hosts 'innovative' Covid vaccine story exhibition |url=https://www.thenational.scot/news/24907220.scottish-museum-hosts-exhibition-race-covid-vaccine/?ref=eb&nid=1907&block=article_block_a&u=6416eeea664393c8b52d25ccceb41c27&date=040225 |access-date=2025-02-04 |website=The National |language=en}}</ref>

==Personal life==
On 11 December 1954 Almeida married Enrique Rosalio (Henry) Almeida (1913–1993), a Venezuelan artist. Together they had a daughter Joyce who became a psychiatrist and had two daughters.<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" />

In 1985, Almeida retired to [[Bexhill-on-Sea]] with her second husband, Phillip Samuel Gardner, a fellow virologist,<ref name="BMJ_Obit_20080418" /> whom she had married in 1979.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=8 October 1994|title=Obituary PS Gardner|url=http://europepmc.org/backend/ptpmcrender.fcgi?accid=PMC2541175&blobtype=pdf|journal=British Medical Journal|volume=309|pages=950–1}}</ref> Gardner died in 1994.<ref name="NYT obit" />

In 2007, Almeida died of a heart attack at Bexhill.<ref name="ODNB_Banatvala_2011_01"/>

==Commemoration==
In September 2020, a new COVID-19 testing laboratory at [[Guy's Hospital]] was named after Almeida.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Trust|first=Guy's and St Thomas's NHS Foundation|title=Guy's Hospital names Covid lab after pioneer who discovered the virus|url=https://www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk/news-and-events/2020-news/september/20200908-guys-hospital-names-covid-lab-after-pioneer-who-discovered-the-virus.aspx|access-date=2020-09-14|website=www.guysandstthomas.nhs.uk|language=en}}</ref>
